forecasts.label: Capital financing requirement
forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

findings.headline: Business rates protection (safety net) tightens from 97% to 92.5% of baseline from 2028/29, reducing downside protection on volatile income.
findings.detail: The council builds business rates into the 2027/28 MTFP at 97% of government baseline—the safety threshold guarantee. The paper notes 'from 2028/29 the safety threshold level decreases to 92.5% of baseline,' reducing the council's downside protection on an already volatile income stream.
findings.matters: This signals gradual withdrawal of government protection and shifting of rate volatility risk back to councils. Councils with weak or volatile business rate bases will feel this acutely. It suggests tightening of financial support across the sector.
findings.quote: It should be noted that from 2028/29 the safety threshold level decreases to 92.5% of baseline.

findings.headline: Investment income falling in Worthing as interest rates drop and capital receipts from property sales decline.
findings.detail: The paper notes 'a reduction in the forecast income from investment, impacted by both a fall in interest rates and the assumed level of capital receipts from the asset disposal programme.' The council earns 3.13% on cash holdings but pays 4.35% on borrowing, creating a structural deficit on cash. Capital receipts (used to fund capital without borrowing) are also falling, forcing more reliance on prudential borrowing.
findings.matters: Councils with significant property portfolios and cash balances are hit twice by the interest rate environment: lower returns on deposits and lower capital receipts from disposals. This signals reduced flexibility to fund capital programmes and therefore rising pressure on prudential borrowing.
findings.figures: Interest yield 3.13%; borrowing cost 4.35%; negative spread 122 basis points
findings.quote: In Worthing this has been compounded by a reduction in the forecast income from investment, impacted by both a fall in interest rates and the assumed level of capital receipts from the asset disposal programme.

findings.headline: Supported accommodation placements have 'increased exponentially' over three years but housing benefit does not cover costs; government has declined targeted funding.
findings.detail: The paper describes 'a disproportionately high allocation of supported accommodation placements (where people receive support, supervision or care), which has increased exponentially over the last 3 years.' The core problem is 'housing benefit not matching housing charges for these placements.' Despite budget increases of £1m in Worthing and £225k in Adur (approved 2025/26), 'the pressure persists.' Officers raised this with MHCLG and DWP but 'there is no indication that any targeted funding will be provided.'
findings.matters: This is distinct from temporary homelessness: it reflects a structural gap in benefits policy where regional care providers commission placements but central housing benefit rates do not cover their cost. It cannot be solved by council action or savings and will persist until central funding changes.
findings.figures: £1m Worthing budget increase 2025/26; £225k Adur; growth 'exponential' over 3 years
findings.quote: Adur and Worthing also have a disproportionately high allocation of supported accommodation placements (where people receive support, supervision or care), which has increased exponentially over the last 3 years, being driven in part by the commissioning decisions of other bodies as well as the underlying impact of housing benefit not matching housing charges for these placements.

findings.headline: Higher interest rates and debt refinancing pushed Worthing financing costs up £1.8m in 2027/28 compared to 2026/27 budget assumptions.
findings.detail: The paper states the increase reflects 'the impact of interest rates higher than assumed in the 2026/27 budget on borrowing, and refinancing requirements.' This is debt that was issued at lower rates maturing and being refinanced at higher rates (4.35% average borrowing assumption for 2027/28). The council is also experiencing this on a capital programme capped at only £1m additional borrowing.
findings.matters: Shows the squeeze on council finances: borrowing costs rising sharply while interest rates remain high. The spread between what councils pay to borrow (4.35%) and earn on cash (3.13%) is 122 basis points, creating a structural headwind. This limits financial flexibility and reduces investment capacity.
findings.figures: £1.8m Worthing; £208k Adur; PWLB assumption 4.6-4.2%; borrowing rate 4.35%; yield on investments 3.13%
findings.quote: the impact of interest rates higher than assumed in the 2026/27 budget on borrowing, and refinancing requirements has increased the financing costs revenue budget requirement in 2027/28 by £1.8m in Worthing and £208k in Adur.

findings.headline: Homelessness spending consuming 37% of Worthing's net revenue budget, with £1.5m continuing overspend despite £2m increase in 2026/27.
findings.detail: The paper projects Worthing spending 37% of its entire net revenue budget on Housing Needs, and Adur 15%. Despite £2m additional investment in Worthing and £400k in Adur (as part of 2026/27 budget), current projections show continuing overspends of £1.5m and £80k respectively. The council explicitly states this is driving need for ongoing EFS and results from demand pressures 'outside of our control.'
findings.matters: Shows even councils willing to invest heavily in homelessness cannot contain costs driven by temporary accommodation demand and housing benefit gaps. This is a sector-wide structural problem, not a management failure. Finance directors at councils with similar demographics will recognise this as intractable without central government action.
findings.figures: 37% of Worthing net budget; 15% of Adur; £1.5m Worthing overspend; £80k Adur overspend; £2m Worthing increase; £400k Adur increase in 2026/27
findings.quote: The councils are seeing sustained and growing pressure for temporary and emergency accommodation and are now forecasting to spend circa 37% of the Worthing and 15% of the Adur net revenue budgets on Housing Needs.
